newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-TYSON TO FACE COMPLAINT CITING FOUL CONDUCT AND DISREPUTE.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-TYSON TO FACE COMPLAINT CITING FOUL CONDUCT AND DISREPUTE.

text.p: Mike Tyson, disqualified for biting Evander Holyfield's ears in their heavyweight title fight, faces a formal complaint alleging unsportsmanlike conduct and bringing boxing into disrepute, prosecutors said Tuesday.

An emergency hearing of the Nevada State Athletic Commission voted unanimously to hold a disciplinary session next week at which the fighter could be heavily fined and or receive a lengthy ban from boxing.
In the meantime, he is temporarily suspended and his nearly $30 million purse from Saturday's fight is being withheld.

"Mike is serious about this, he will place his fate in their hands," Tyson's lawyer, Eckley Keach, told reporters after Tuesday's public hearing. "Mike is willing to accept whatever the commission determines."
Tuesday's meeting of the five-man commission began with a playing of the videotape of the World Boxing Association bout in which Tyson was disqualified for biting Holyfield twice in the third round.

Holyfield, who had beaten Tyson in their first bout in November, required 15 stitches in his right ear and will have to undergo reconstructive plastic surgery to repair a hole in the top of it. His left ear was extensively chewed, but there was no permanent damage, doctors said.
The champion's lawyer has said he has not ruled out filing civil charges against Tyson for the bites.

After watching all three rounds of the fight and the ensuing melee in the ring after the disqualification, commission member Jim Nave read a motion formally asking for the District Attorney's office to draw up a complaint against Tyson.

The commission ordered the fight's promoter, Don King Productions, to provide a check for $29,824,600, representing Tyson's purse, to be deposited in an interest-bearing account pending the outcome of the hearing.
Once the Nevada attorney general's office drew up a formal complaint, a period of three working days must pass before the hearing may be held.
That would set the hearing for next Tuesday or Wednesday at the earliest, since the July 4 Independence Day holiday is observed on Friday.

Keach told the commission that Tyson waived the 30-day period he is allowed under the regulations to address a complaint so that the issue can be settled as quickly as possible. Tyson had said as much Monday in a public apology.

Deputy District attorney Joe Rolston told reporters that two state code violations would be involved in the complaint, one alleging that Tyson is "guilty of foul or unsportsmanlike conduct," and the other alleging the fighter is "guilty of conduct which discredits boxing."

Since the complaint does not involve criminal charges, it does not represent a violation of Tyson's parole from a rape conviction in Indiana. The fighter served three years in jail for the 1991 crime and was placed on four year's probation when released in March 1995.
Tyson did not attend the emergency hearing held at the Las Vegas Council Chambers in City Hall, but his lawyer, Keach said: If it is in his interests to attend (next week), he will."
Keach referred to the boxer's public apology and said: "There is no way we are going to argue that he shouldn't be fined or suspended."

Rolston said Tyson could be fined a maximum of $250,000, or be both fined and suspended by the commission. If Tyson's license is revoked, the boxer could be fined up to 10 percent of his purse, or nearly $3 million.
Tyson pleaded for his professional future Monday when he apologised for "snapping" in the ring and begged forgiveness.
He said he would accept the punishment to be handed down, asking only that it not be a lifetime ban from boxing.
Tyson, who turned 31 Monday, explained away his action by saying he was angered over a cut he sustained in a head-butting clash in the second round that was ruled unintentional.

"I apologise to the world, to my family and to the Nevada State Athletic Commission that has always treated me fairly," Tyson said in the prepared statement that was seen by many boxing insiders as a calculated appeal for clemency.
He also acknowledged that he was seeking psychiatric help to try and control his actions.
Tyson's lawyer said that in his own opinion the disqualification was sufficent punishment for Tyson.
"There's been a rush to judgment in the media and the press, I've been reading so much in the press that Mike should be banned or whatever," Keach said, calling for "a fair disposition of the case."
But he stressed it was his own opinion and that Tyson himself was prepared to accept whatever punishment was meted out.
Asked Tyson's reaction to President Clinton saying he and all Americans were "horrified" by the ear-biting, Keach snapped: "Well, Mike hasn't heard from Bill telling him he was horrified, all right?"
